name: Self-renewing hull coat
subtitle: a living paint that keeps a hull clean

effects.effect: a cell can run on a genome written entirely by computer
microscopic bumps make water bead up and roll off, carrying dirt away
capsules in a plastic burst when it cracks and glue the crack shut

effect: a cell can run on a genome written entirely by computer
how: Barnacles and weed on a hull add up to several percent of world shipping fuel, and the paints that stop them work by slowly leaching poison into the sea. A coat seeded with a contained marine bacterium that continuously secretes a slippery polymer renews its own surface instead of wearing out, and regrows over a scrape rather than leaving bare metal. The organism is built to need a nutrient held in the coating, so it dies where the coating ends.
obstacle: A coating that must stay alive for five years between dry-dockings, in freezing water and tropical sun, is a tall order.
why: Slippery coatings and contained microbes both exist; keeping them alive on a hull doesn't.
real: An ONR-funded Essex project is developing self-repairing engineered-biofilm hull coatings, UNSW encapsulated the antifouling bacterium Pseudoalteromonas tunicata in a 'living paint' lab prototype, and a 2025 paper assembles non-GM biofilm coatings, but field durability is unsolved and no working self-renewing coat exists.
